title: Studying with Stefan Wolpe and meeting John Carisi
summary: Wolpe opens a world of twelve-tone music, and he sends Carisi to him.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: You had talked in that Metronome article about the things that George Handy was doing for Boyd Raeburn were things that--
It was a different approach in each case, but that was there to be done, I guess, at that time.
I had begun studying with Stefan Wolpe about that same time, late '45, and that opened up a whole world to me, but before that there was always a curiosity of how does
* Krzysztof Penderecki, composer of atonal music.

this work. What Bartok and Stravinsky were doing in those days was not I might have been used to hearing. How that fit into the total thing fascinated me and I did want to learn about it. I wanted to learn about [Schoenberg] Shurenberg (phonetic spelling); I never got quite to Shurenberg. It never turned me on the way the other did; it still doesn't.
Wolpe was a twelve tone writer, but what a good teacher, what an inspiration- al human being he was.
Apparently Charlie Parker had gone to him and asked for lessons.
John came from McKinley's band; he had been up at Yale with Miller and Miller didn't take him overseas because (inaudible), so Ray got him back to
write for him, and that's where I met Johnny and encouraged him to go to Stefan, which he did. He says he's always been grateful to me for that. I don't know why but he has been.
